utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, and Daryl Mundis, assisted by Mr. Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel and Stefane Bourgon co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 208th day of our hearings, I greet everyone present. Members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, General Hadzihasanovic, Brigadier Kubura. And I would not like to forget to greet everyone else present in the courtroom and around the courtroom. The Trial Chamber would like to ask Defence counsel whether they would agree, perhaps not now, but after the break and in the following days, to change position. Because Brigadier Kubura's Defence counsel is examining witnesses, so it would be better for you to be in the front row so that you could have closer contact with the witness. This could be done after the break. It's not necessary to do this now. I think that would be preferable, otherwise you're too far away. Having said that, I will now ask the registrar to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we are in open session, I will ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called here as a as a witness for Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel. Before you take the solemn declaration could you please tell me your first and last name, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dzemail Ibranovic, son of Zina [phoen], born on the 22nd of October 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you by profession, if you are currently employed. If you have a profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a religious cleric in the Islamic community in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, were you employed? Did you have a position of any kind? And if you were in the ABiH, which unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As other members of the clergy, I was in Brajici when the war broke out and I joined the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993? Or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Defence counsel who will commence their examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we will be following here. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel. You have certainly met them already before this hearing. Defence counsel have told us that they will need an hour, hour and a half for their examination-in-chief. Perhaps less. But this is a rough estimate. Once this stage has been completed, you will have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution who are to your right. The Prosecution will conduct what we call their cross-examination and they will have the same amount of time as Defence counsel. Then defence counsel may put additional questions to you. The three Judges who are sitting before you may ask you questions at any point in time, but the Judges prefer to wait for the parties to put all their questions to you before we put our questions to you in order to clarify some of your answers or because we believe that there are certain gaps that need to be filled in the interest of justice. Under such conditions we might feel it necessary to put questions to you. There are two things I want to point out that concern our procedure. As you have just taken the solemn declaration, this means that you should not give false testimony, but this is something you are certainly aware of. In addition, there is a fairly complicated provision that I must inform witnesses of. If you believe that you should not answer a question because it could be used against you at a subsequent date you may refuse to answer such a question. Such cases have never arisen to date, but in such a case the Trial Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question, but the witness is guaranteed immunity. The procedure followed here is Anglo-Saxon. The procedure is almost completely oral, and that is why your testimony is so important. When you speak, whatever you say is transcribed and interpreted. You may also be shown documents and asked to identify the documents or to comment on some of the documents. If the questions put to you seem too complicated or confused, don't hesitate to ask the party putting the question to you to rephrase the question. If you encounter any difficulties in the course of the proceedings, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We're here to deal with any difficulties that may arise. In about one hour and 25 minutes, we will have a break so that you can have a rest because, as you will realise, to answer questions incessantly can be quite tiring. We will then have a 20 or 25-minute break and after the break we will resume and continue working for an hour and a half. If everyone adheres to the schedule, to won't be necessary for you to remain in The Hague tomorrow. Hopefully we will be able to complete your testimony today. Without wasting any more time I will now give the floor to Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel who will commence their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have started a little late, I will try to be expeditious and apart from a few general questions, I will limit myself to the counts in the indictment that this witness could testify about. Mr. Ibranovic, you've already said that in 1992 you became a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade. When was this?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The unit was established as the situation unfolded we were not prepared when the war broke out and I, as a member of the clergy, would never have believed that such a situation could arise. So initially there were these guard patrols and I became part of those guard patrols in our community at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When exactly did you become a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Well, the 7th Muslim Brigade, when it was being formed, I was in the Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Was that in November 1993 -- 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: 1992? I think it was in the second half of that month. It was cold. We were holding the lines after the fall of Jajce at that time, a very tumultus time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any particular establishment post within the first battalion, any particular duties that you had to perform?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Assistant commander for morale in the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when you were appointed as assistant commander for morale and religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I think it was around March.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, could you say in which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993. As assistant commander for morale, you were the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs. So could you tell us what sort of duties you had to perform?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I think that everyone knows that this unit followed the rules and regulations of Islam. Our purpose was to inform all the fighters of the basic rules. This meant informing them of how to maintain their personal hygiene and how to maintain their purity, their spiritual purity. It's not just a matter of a soldier knowing how to perform the rites. It's also a matter of informing them how to protect themselves from envy, hatred, during that extremely difficult period of time. These duties involved instructing the soldiers in the field of religion, in that field of religion, and naturally one had to spend time with the troops, that was very important. Sometimes if someone who was involved in these matters simply appeared, that was very important for the soldiers, even if you didn't tell them anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, given what you have just said, you mentioned teachings, et cetera. You're a member of the clergy. We've already discussed these matters. Could you tell us what sort of educational background you have.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Well, before the war I graduated from the Faculty of Islam in Sarajevo, the Islam Theological Faculty as it was called at the time. And even before that I became involved in another field of activity, in learning the Koran by heart. I completed that training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of education do you have now, as far as that area is concerned?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: After the war, I wrote a masters thesis. I'm now writing my Ph.D. thesis on a certain fraternity, a Sufi fraternity, Nex Appendi [phoen]. I'm from the Central Bosnian area and this tradition, the tradition of fraternities has taken root in that area. And that is a tradition that I feel spiritually akin to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I've already shown you this booklet. The instructions to the Muslim fighter. P11 is the exhibit number. You've had a look at it and you've read it. Could you comment on it, and could you first tell me whether you've ever seen this booklet. Did you ever see the booklet before I showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I saw it in the course of the war. I saw many other such booklets in the course of the war. There's no censorship. Anyone could write whatever they wanted to write. This was not something that -- it was obligatory to read. And from a scientific point of view, since I'm now involved in scientific work, I can tell you that there are many things that could be objected to in this booklet, because if something is to be regarded as a serious literary work or a serious work of science, it has to have a solid basis. The relevant literature must be referred to. I do not have such sources so anyone could have written almost anything. Anyone could have expressed their point of view. And naturally this was not binding on anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the clergy and as the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, did you ever provide any sort of instruction based on this booklet?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Someone who has graduated from the theological faculty will use books and won't use booklets of this kind in the course of his lectures, but if I had used such booklets, if someone used these booklets, that would show his degree of education, his degree of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This booklet or these instructions, whatever we call it, was it something that members of the 7th Muslim Brigade had to have and had to read?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Well, naturally that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ibranovic, I would now like to move on to another subject, since in 1993 you were in Travnik. So I would first like to ask you whether you've ever heard of the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The village of Miletici is about 15 kilometres from the community that I worked in. And at the time I wasn't even aware of the existence of that hamlet because it was never necessary for me to go there. It was only after all of those events that I heard about it and I heard about the events that had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When these events occurred in Miletici - perhaps I could put a leading question to the witness - it was on the 24th of April, 1993. When these events occurred, where were you?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I was in my community, in the Alihodza community.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in the village of Alihodza when you arrived there were there any other members of the 7th Muslim Brigade in your village or in the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Before I arrived there, I spent a lengthy period of time, perhaps about a month in Bijelo Buca at the front line or in the town of Travnik, and I was supposed to go and leave, to have a rest. I was in Travnik when these events occurred, when the events occurred in Ahmici. And then after a telephone conversation with my wife, I was told that the situation was deteriorating in my community, around my community, and I felt that I should return rapidly, which is what I did. I returned with some of the members of the young men from the area, from those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just clarify where exactly it was that you returned to, you and those young men.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: So I got to Alihodza. Facing Alihodza - and you can see it on the map - is a village called Kljaci. In that village there were about ten members of our battalion. So it was after Ahmici and before Miletici, that sort of time scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And those members of the 7th Muslim Brigade who were in your village or in the village of Kljaci, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As a rule we had to -- or rather the weapons had to be left, either at the front lines or at the command, depending on who did what.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you reply once again. I believe that it has gone into the transcript already. Your village of Alihodza and the village of Kljaci are very close to one another, well, facing one another. How far are they from one another? How far is it from Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I think seven to eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: About your village or the village of Kljaci or in the Biljanska Valley, was there an organised unit of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: There was no organised units, but we had young men from those villages who would come to Travnik and be distributed according to needs, and then they would go back to their own villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When they were on leave, they would go back to their own villages?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us for how long you stayed in your village of Alihodza and, if you know, the same about the others who were in the neighbouring village of Kljaci?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I would say throughout that period until -- until the final conflict. I was in that, my community of origin, in the same way as those young men. And people are not used to war. They were frightened. Apart from that, I had my own family there and, quite simply, I just joined in with the rest of them in forming the lines above Alihodza in that forest, because above that village the HVO was already forming their lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in terms of time, if I'm not mistaken, you said sometime mid April, and then until when did you stay in the area?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Throughout that period until we got the order to go to Kiseljak. And that meant the end of the operations in that area. I think mid-June.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When did you go back to Travnik for the first time?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: To the battalion? Oh, with that piece of news, well I heard and I was just standing in front of my house and I was told we were going to Kiseljak, and I was kind of pleased, because that's where I was born, in that area. So when I got to Travnik, things continued like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In this period when you said you were there, on the 24th of April, did you go to the village of Miletici and have you ever been to the village of Miletici at all in that period?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The hamlet of Alihodza is a small hamlet, some 15 houses, 20 at most. And in the beginning, because there were very few of us, well, we held that line for eight hours. So there was no question of us going nowhere else. And any movement would have been difficult, because if you take a look at the map, you will see that, that road from Alihodza in the direction of Mehurici, there could have been snipers there, and people used to get killed there, and there were people who were wounded there. So you could only go there at night or during the daytime if there was fog.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So neither you yourself nor -- and can you tell us about the other members who were at that village of Kljaci. Do you know whether any of them had gone there at that period?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I'm talking about this critical day, the 24th of April. We were all basically chained our own -- chained to our own door steps because it was about defending our own homes at the time. And it would have been illogical, and my own wife mentioned that to me in that phone conversation, it would have been illogical for me to spend time somewhere else. And HVO was basically on our own door step. There were shots being fired already.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As to the escalation of this conflict at the beginning of June, 1993, did it find you in your own village again? Did you, at any point in time, find out about the whereabouts of the 7th Muslim Brigade in the beginning of June 1993 and whether they have actively participated in any of those actions?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Since I was linked to that line -- well, it would take up too much time if I were to tell you all the details at this stage. Of course I was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in my own community. I found people there who were the representatives of the authorities. But as to war, up until then it had not been felt in the area. And my assistance there basically consisted of the take digging of the ditches and setting up of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, you misunderstood me. What I asked you was if at some point in time later you found out where the 1st battalion was involved there, in what sort of activity?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: After the end, since the communication lines were disrupted I couldn't go to Travnik and none of them could visit me. I found out all the details later on, how things happened and what in way and everything when we were about to go to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of the people that you talked to.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: One of our commanders, a company commanders, Suad Jusovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Suad Jusovic told you where the first battalion was involved in combat activity?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: That's at the area around Travnik. Hajdareve Njive, at the area of Sibicara. And then we -- there were further operations Mjavin [phoen], Jajce, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the question from the counsel. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the entry in Travnik, as you go from Sarajevo to the right, there is a slope where the HVO had their lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript. My question wasn't there. However, the interpreters did not hear it. I asked about where exactly the Hajdareve Njive village was and the witness has just answered. You mentioned Sibicara, there were combat activities there. Where exactly is Sibicara, what part of the Travnik municipality is it?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It is opposite Hajdareve Njive. Once again, very near to Travnik. Hajdareve Njive is to the right and Sibicara is to the left. It's an area which is called, and it used to be called in that way in the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, and there was a factory built there at the time and it is still called Sibicara, even though -- oh, it was a factory for the manufacturing of matches and now very few of such articles are being produced there. But those are slopes which are very close together. But they are facing one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: I can see on the transcript that the names of the localities have not been made clear. Could you ask the witness to repeat the name of the villages or to spell the name of the villages please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, you've heard what the Judge has just said. Could you spell the name of the village Sibicara?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: S-i-b-i-c-a-r-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you mention the name of the place, you said that it was a synonym for "match factory."

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer did not appear in the transcript. When you talk about the place called Sibicara what you had in mind was the production plant for matches at Travnik?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes. And the area surrounding the factory where the HVO had their lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, I'm going to ask you something else now. Have you ever met foreigners -- some people called them Mujahedin. Others called them Asian-African country soldiers, fighters. Have you ever met them anywhere in Travnik or in the area of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did come across them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever had any contacts with those foreigners?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Their arrival, in as far as our people were concerned, was kind of interesting. But very soon I realised that our views of certain matters were worlds apart. An educated man and somebody who has some knowledge of theology cannot go along with the reasoning of a hand labourer, no matter where that person comes from. What I mean by this is certain interpretations of Islam, because of which they've created huge difficulties for us in our own communities. Since I myself am one of the clergy who used to work at one of these communities, I could not accept those things. So that we had differing views and we didn't have lots of contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And this contact that you were referring to earlier on, did you meet them in private? Or was it within the framework of what you did as the assistant commander for moral and religious issues?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Those are things related to religion, to faith. For example, in the course of the ritual washing, I wash my neck as well, and they could come along and tell me that I shouldn't be doing that, that that is not allowed. And I do know that he has no real argument on which to base that comment. Obviously we can't find a common denominator. I'm just quoting this as one example. Quite apart from the fact that when it comes to the very understanding of Islam, all those who study Islam know that there are different ideas. We could divide them into somewhat softer approaches, such as Sufija [phoen], and I have already mentioned that I was from that area, and somewhat similar extreme approaches that tend to come from the east. And those two different views of Islam simply can't go together. In this respect, I have undertaken to work on my doctorate in connection with this one, Sufism.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, have you had frequent contacts with the soldiers, members of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: In as far as the circumstances allowed, because I was -- as most of my -- as most of our soldiers, I was involved in two different things. On the one hand, I had my family. On the other hand, I had the community. And then the fighters. And I did what I could. But the time was as it was. And all that was indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that those foreign fighters were at Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I had heard that they did snoop around that area and that they moved about. I mean they had not actually links to any specific area. That's the sort of people who don't really fit into any system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, did they have any links with that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest of the phrase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we had our own command and all the needs that we had to deal with, we could deal with through our command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My question was, for the sake of the transcript, was the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade -- have any links with the Mehurici camp? Your answer has already gone into the transcript. Thank you. Mr. Ibranovic -- and now I would like to move on to an altogether different topic. I think we have dispensed with this one. In November 1993, were you in the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you, before this Trial Chamber, tell us for what reason you went there and how you got there.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: After the massacre at Stupni Do perpetrated by the HVO, we got the orders to move in that direction. The entire brigade was directed to do so and we came from the direction of Breza. We were stationed in a village which is called Strijezevo. My battalion, the 1st Battalion, went through the valley. There was no combat activity because the HVO had withdrawn so that we could enter without any fighting. We could enter the town itself without any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally in the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many soldiers of the 1st Battalion entered the city of Vares and did they enter the city of Vares at all?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: We were at the gates of the city. I don't know what the name of the place was, An or Majdan, I don't know exactly. A couple of us, members of the 1st Battalion went in. I was especially interested in the mosque, of course, myself. And from the lower part of town I walked to the upper town. As to soldiers, not too many. Perhaps fifty or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What did Vares look like when you entered the town itself?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It looked deserted and here and there I met a couple of members of the local police. In the upper part of town, I remember, I think two buildings were on fire. They were new buildings. I didn't see civilians at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you and that group of soldiers - if I've understood you correctly it was about 50 soldiers - how long did you stay in the town of Vares itself?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Very briefly. By sunset we had left the centre of town and had gone back to Strijezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the rest of the 1st Battalion, why didn't they enter the town?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Look, there was military police and they controlled the comings and goings and most probably I wouldn't have been allowed to go in, had I not been a member of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And the same situation applied to when you left Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And did the police officers at that checkpoint carry out any controls? Did they carry out controls with regard to soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that those soldiers that went in, that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Again, we did not hear the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I will repeat my question. When you entered the town of Vares and when the soldiers were there, did you notice the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade looting or stealing any of the property from Vares? Were they looting in this town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: What could a soldier have put into his bag? Well, that's a very delicate matter. It's true to say that in Central Bosnia people were going hungry. And given what I could observe, the town of Vares was full of food and I had the impression that it was more necessary than the weapons themselves. If anyone could have taken anything, then they took whatever would fit into a military bag, so judge for yourself what could have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned food. Could you just explain what you meant when you said "food".

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Food. Oil. Flour. Sugar. Staple items. As a souvenir I took a bottle opener but I lost it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did the military police check people at the exits from the town of Vares to see whether anyone had taken or misappropriated property?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Naturally. It was quite normal to expect such situations since from the very beginning of the conflict with the HVO this area had been closed off and, in some areas, there was a shortage of such goods. There was a black marketeering, looting, and that was to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did the military police prevent such acts?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the other Defence team have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We have a few questions for Mr. Ibranovic. On the whole, the questions have to do with clarifying some of the answers given to my learned colleague. Could the witness first be shown DH52 [Realtime transcript read in error "D852"], which is a map, which would help the Trial Chamber understand the witness's location.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH52. Not 8-5-2. DH52. I have the map on me. Other witnesses have marked it. I don't want the witness to comment on it. But perhaps the witness could just indicate his location on the map. Could we place this map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, while the map is being placed on the ELMO, I would just like to tell you that the questions I put to you might be somewhat different from the questions put to you by my learned colleague. I am allowed to put leading questions to you and you can just answer my questions by saying "yes" or "no." Naturally if there is anything that you would like to add, you may naturally do so. In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague you said that at sometime after the events in Ahmici, sometime after the 16th of April, you and a group of combatants and -- who were from the village of Alihodza arrived in the village of Alihodza. Could you please use the pointer. You will be provided with to indicate on the map the location of the villages of Alihodza and Kljaci. These are villages you mentioned when talking about your presence during that period of time in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the village of Kljaci, and here on the opposite side, on the map, it says "Brajici," but that's the name for three hamlets. One of them is marked here it says "Karahodze." In the middle we have Alihodza, and further above we have Zolote. These are three old tribes so to speak that have been living there for centuries. This place is known as Alihodza because an old Bosnian family, Ali Hodza lived there. But when Austria arrived, all these three hamlets were called Brajici.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly, you said that you and comrades in arms arrived there in that village, or rather in the surroundings of that village, and you were there on the 24th of April when these events in Miletici took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you use the map to show where Miletici is located in relation to your village.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's where it is. Mr. Ibranovic, if I understood you correctly, you said that although you worked in your community near Alihodza. Before the war you had never been to the village of Miletici and you weren't aware of its existence?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that in your village, in the village of Alihodza, not far from Plijaka [phoen] [Realtime transcript read in error "Klaka"], you were there at the time of combat at the beginning of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The transcript doesn't reflect the names of the places. Page 23, line 1, "from Klaka."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I asked whether it would also be correct to say or rather I asked whether I had understood you correctly, did you say that you in the village of Alihodza and in the surroundings of Kljaci, were you there all the time in the course of the combat in the Bila valley at the beginning of June; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have explained to us where Hajdareve Njive in the Sibicara were located, could you use the map to show us the exact locations of Hajdareve Njive and Sibicara?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: At the very entrance to Travnik you have Dolac marked in red here. To the right when you enter Travnik, there is a slope called Hajdareve Njive. The HVO held their lines there. To the left and below there is a small hill and the HVO also held its lines there. And just a little below we have Sibicara. The people still call that area Sibicara to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, tell me was that in fact the position held by the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade? It was subsequently explained to you by the company commander, Mr. Jusovic.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that -- that your position and the position of some of the members of the 1st Battalion is clearer to me now. I now have some questions that have to do with your establishment post of assistant commander from morale and religious affairs. Would you agree with me, Mr. Ibranovic, if I said that the ABiH had very clear rules on the freedom of individuals to practice various religions within the army?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally this concerned members of the Catholic, Orthodox, Jewish, and Muslim confession. Is that correct? As a highly educated theologian, could you confirm that Islam in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been a religion of tolerance for centuries in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a religion which advocated living together with other faiths in the area?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, could you also confirm that many ordinary people, religious people and people who weren't religious, were surprised by the cruelty shown, the cruel attitude shown towards religious edifices of that people and towards the religion of that people?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your duties and as an ordinary man, did you ever feel and were you ever given strict orders, according to which our soldiers and the people as a whole, should not retaliate in kind, should not treat other religious buildings in the way that Islamic buildings had been treated in that area?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The rules of Islam are quite clear, as far as that is concerned. Mustafa Hamed [phoen] over 1.400 years ago quite clearly said that women, children, the helpless should not be touched. As far as tolerance is concerned, or at least as far as my area is concerned, tolerance was so great that, for example, for a member of the Sufi faith, there was -- there were items for religious rites in a Catholic house. There was water. There were -- there was a towel, because the Catholics considered such people to be holy people.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, a lot of evidence presented before this Chamber indicates that in the area of Central Bosnia, mosques were destroyed in Ahmici and Donje Bandol. Since the 7th Muslim Brigade was composed of fighters who were religious men, you as the commander for morale, did you tell the soldiers that they should not treat the religious edifices in this way, and did you ever observe or did you ever notice that members of the 7th Muslim Brigade had desecrated or damaged buildings belonging to other ethnic groups, churches, cemeteries?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: They were all familiar with the code of conduct and if they committed such acts, they were aware of the fact that they would be held to account.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, did you, in the battalion, also receive clear orders from your superior command according to which religious buildings and members of the clergy should be given particular protection?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, did members of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade adhere to these orders, did they abide by these orders?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is not an objection, but members of the 7th Muslim Brigade are not accused of having committed acts of any kind against religious edifices. That is all that I wanted to point out. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean to suggest that they had been accused of that. I just wanted to hear, from a highly educated imam, what the attitude of religious people was and they weren't only religious people in the 7th Muslim Brigade. You tried to answer that question, so with the Trial Chamber's leave I would ask you to please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As far as I know there were no such excesses. They had been warned and we all knew about these things, given the way in which we had been brought up.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few more questions with regard to your duties as assistant commander for morale and religious affairs. You have told the Chamber that you were involved in religious affairs and religious instruction. But you also said it was very important for you to spend time among the troops because your presence among them raised their morale and you taught them not to hate and not to be afraid. My question is as follows: In the course of your duties, did you try to instill patriotic feelings in the soldiers? Did you try to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. encourage them to defend their country, their people and their religion?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary to tell them about such things. We all were fully aware of the situation we were in. We had to decide whether to stay and attend like Palestinians or to defend one's home in which, God willing, our children would be able to live, would be free to live.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, tell me whether within that department from morale, were you also involved in certain social affairs; for example, assistance for the wounded, for families of members of the clergy, or did your duties only involve religious instruction?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Naturally everything that had to do with wounded men or the families of men who had been killed, we would visit these families, if that was possible and provide them with assistance to the extent that was possible. Usually we would provide them with goods. So that is how we would visit them.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Instilling a feeling of patriotism in the troops, taking care of the wounded and of the families of men who had been killed, were these duties the duties that you had to perform within the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now 11.20. I think it would be best to have our break now and the Prosecution will then commence with its cross-examination. It is now 11.20. We will resume at about ten to 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume, and I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning. My name is Matthias Neuner I'm appearing here along with my colleagues on behalf of the Prosecution and I will put a couple of questions to you. If you don't understand any of these questions please ask me to repeat it and I will do so and I am also prepared to rephrase the question, if necessary. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to take you to Vares. You testified on page 18 that "We got the orders to move in that direction," meaning moving to Vares, and the and I wanted to ask you who gave you, at the end of 1993, the order to wanted to ask you who gave you, at the end of 1993, the order to move to Vares.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Within the chain of command we were under the brigade command. We act in accordance with orders issued by the brigade command, and the order stated that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was to engage in the direction of the town of Vares itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was issuing this order? Was it your battalion commander or was it the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The brigade commander issues orders that are forwarded to battalion commanders and then the battalion commander distributes the orders in the various departments. For example, in my -- in the department for morale. So that the troops can then be informed of the situation, we then express our opinion on the situation in terms of the morale of the troops, in terms of whether we can set off to carry out the task or to see whether any other preparations are necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just for the record, do you know the name of the commander who issued the initial order?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I can talk about my own level, the level of battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Junozovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Jusovic"] was the commander of the 1st Battalion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in the wider Vares area, at what time was it, if you can try to recall.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It was in the autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, it says "Jusovic." Line 20 -- page 29. It should say "Junozovic." That's line six.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can clarify. Will you please repeat the first name and the last name of the battalion commander who issued the order.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Safet Junozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please spell Junozovic for the record.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: J-u-n-o-z-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Junozovic --

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It's one word. It hasn't been written down quite correctly it's been separated. In fact that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Junosovic, he was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What time did you arrive in the wider Vares area, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Perhaps it was in the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... of October?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It was rainy. I don't know when it was exactly though, I don't want to guess the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned Strijezevo. And just for clarification, Strijezevo, is this a hamlet near mount Trebijas [phoen], about seven kilometres south of Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It's a village at the entrance to Vares near Breza. Perhaps that is the distance. It's on the left side of the road. I wasn't very familiar with that area. I was slightly familiar with the area -- THE. INTERPRETER: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because when I went to secondary school, I spent some time in a village near Brijezovo [phoen] that was in 1982. I went to the second class of the madrasa, the religious school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in Strijezevo, before you decided to go to Vares, did you meet anybody from the command of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The command of the 1st Battalion was located in a summer house. And given the communication I had with the members of the command, there was the assistant commander for morale there, Kurtanovic, Sulejman Kurtanovic. We assistant commanders from the battalion had meetings with him, and we discussed the current situation and how the situation was developing. We discussed what should be done and how it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what conclusion emerged out of this discussion? Can you please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Well, there was a surprise. Most people were surprised because the town was taken without a fight. And since the town was full of food and naturally the soldiers needed food, this is the subject that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you just said the soldiers needed food and you discussed it. Can you please elaborate a little bit. What was the course of action decided upon?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: We were surprised. I did say that before. Even if at that time one wanted to provide for the soldiers, we did not have the necessary infrastructure. We did not have any trucks to carry the food. So we talked about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what was the solution? The solution was to order some trucks or what was the solution taken? You said you didn't have any trucks at the time, but you were organising some?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As far as I know, very few, because we got to that area from Zenica and we came by train to Visoko, I believe, and then we travelled by busses part of the way and then we walked. So we came from the opposite side, as it were. The other side of the hill, as you said, you said the name of the mountain. From where the logistical support was, so we had very little in the way of logistical support. Perhaps we had a small car or a small utility vehicle because we had basically walked there, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just said you walked there and you described the little bit. Is it correct to summarise this. You took the main road through Vares Majdan from the south and you entered Vares? Is this a correct description?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And how many cars did you take with you or trucks, or did you just walk by foot?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: If there were any vehicles, there was one vehicle belonging to the battalion command and I had the opportunity to ride in that vehicle as well. Very often -- I mean, for the most part we had a Jeep. And I don't know exactly at what distance I myself travelled by that car, because I know I walked into town on foot. The situation was not altogether safe. One had to watch out because there could have been shots coming from someplace. So in that case of semi-occupation or -- we were a bit careful. And we were surprised that there was no shooting, but it was obvious that the warehouses were full of food, and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did you or your colleagues, I mean the officers with you, did you inspect some of these full warehouses once you had entered Vares town?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I remember I turned off. Because that's a very narrow road. It's in a ravine. So there's no width to speak of. All you can see are the buildings alongside the road and then you walk down the main road and then you can basically see the doors of some of those cellars, and I opened some of those doors and I could see what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what was the situation you just mentioned? So the cellars were full with certain food items or -- please just describe; how many cellars did you see?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I've mentioned this. I mean, my main intention was one and one only. I wanted to check out the state of the mosque. And you have to go -- walk up from the lower side of the town to the upper town. So you go through the entire city centre and perhaps I saw one or two cellars on my way, and -- I mean, I wasn't particularly curious or anything, because I had no opportunity to take anything -- anything that was there anyway. You could take a look and see what the situation was and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier about 50 soldiers were with you entering Vares town. Did they stay with you while you were visiting the mosque? Or did they go somewhere else in town?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they stayed back in the lower part of town. I checked out the mosque and it was all right and then I went back and I found them down there opposite us, as it were. There was the -- where the UNPROFOR people, they had armoured vehicles and tanks and they were looking at us and we were looking at them. And one of those people came up, and I remember this quite well because those two buildings I mentioned, newish buildings, were on fire. And the whole thing was rather chaotic and this man said, and it was nothing strange. I mean for them to say so, he said "This is your country. You have to keep it safe or guard it." I mean, he might have thought that we might destroy something or whatever. But we stayed there for a very short period of time. If you just think of the fact that we entered the town in the afternoon and before sunset we had already gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name or maybe, if you don't remember the name, the nationality of this UNPROFOR person who spoke with your group on that day?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And we are talking about one particular day from early morning to the sunset you said. Do you have an idea whether it was the 3rd of November, was it the 4th of November? Was it another day? Please try to recall. I'm referring to 1993.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: What I do remember clearly is that -- I mean, that's the way we experienced it. Since that was the first liberated town, from our point of view, our own service was working on a programme that we were going to implement and carry out at that particular mosque. We wanted to provide some moral support and give some incentive to people to come back and start normal life. And that day, the day after, I mean, was a Friday. And I know this for a fact because there was a central event there on Friday which was called Djuma and after that Djuma we carried out this programme that we had. So this is all easy to check, if you look at the calendar. And after Djuma, we were addressed by someone from the ministry, the then-ministry, Rusmir Mahmutcehajic and he was there with the local dignitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you just clarify. On the Thursday you entered and left Vares town, that's what I understood. But this celebration, or Djuma you just mentioned, was this the next day, a Friday and so you returned to Vares for a short while to attend this Djuma? Can you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes. But I think that there were no armed forces present, because they had to leave. It was a ceremony marking the liberation of the town, and we just wanted the people to see that that was the start of normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just mentioned there was -- there was somebody from the ministry, "and I got hold of an article which was written in the bulletin of the 37th Muslim Light Brigade, on the 1st of January, 1995. And it is called 'taking Fatih's path.'" And I just want to mention one little portion of it. It says here that: After a short recovery - meaning after the Vares operation. I quote now, beginning of quote, "after a short recovery, the unit prepares for a festive review when President Alija Izetbegovic visited". The location isn't mentioned here in the article. I think it is authored by yourself. But may I just ask for clarification: Was this review in Zenica, which was attended by Alija Izetbegovic? Or did this review take place somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes, that was in Zenica and afterwards as well, after Vares. To be a bit more specific, it was perhaps sometime between the 5th and 7th of December, as far as I can remember. Yeah, that's correct; I'm the author of that text. It was an article illustrating the events that were taking place there. I mean, of course I was not present on every occasion, but I talked to the fighters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you attended also this review by Alija Izetbegovic in Zenica? I think it was in the sports hall in Zenica, but please clarify for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was there. I think it was at the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You want to say something?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes. Certain prizes were awarded and awards were given to certain fighters, so we had to prepare for that. It was a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I can just for one second go back to this article again. It says here, and I quote: "Following an order from" -- I think it is -- I will start again. I think this is relating to another incident, and I quote here: "Following an order from Bjelovac, the battalion heads for Fojnica via Mount Zahor. At the entrance to Fojnica, Izetbegovic and his entourage pass by the unit." And I believe you're talking about the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade. But can you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my area. That's where I come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I'm not entitled to ask a question here, but I do not understand the questions being asked by our learned colleague at the moment, and they have nothing to do with the questions asked by the other Defence team, by my questions, by the indictment, or by anything that the witness has said so far. Perhaps he should first establish a link with the questions he is putting to the witness now. Is it just coming out of the blue? Or does it have anything to do with the actual facts that the Prosecution is trying to prove?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The witness has just said that Mr. Izetbegovic reviewed the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in Zenica, I believe from 3 to 5 December 1993, and I'm just trying to establish the temporal link between this review and the other portion mentioned in the article. And since we have the author sitting here, I thought he could shed some light on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I don't quite see is the link between the visit of Mr. Izetbegovic in December and Vares. Yes, the Defence please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my learned colleague has just mentioned an article. I don't know whether it is Prosecution exhibit or what. Perhaps if they could tell us so we can follow it. If it's a new document, then you will have to rule and the Prosecution will have to stick by your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's speed things up here. Now, this document, is it a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, which the Prosecution doesn't seek to introduce at this stage, is, indeed, a new document. It has been disclosed to both Defence counsels this Monday, meaning far beyond the 24-hour time period to which the Prosecution is obliged. And in line with your decision on memory refreshment, I'm just asking the witness whether he could tell us something about what he wrote in the year 1995 on the 1st of January. That's all the Prosecution tries to establish. It is not intended at all to introduce this article into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've mentioned that that's my birth place. And that's why it says, the path of Fatih, that's where we went, the Sultan, Fatih the 2nd, who ruled between 1443 and -- well, or in that year, in that area of Milodrasko Polje where there was a residence of the Bosnian king, allowed the then-keeper of the military monastery to issue a document with regard to the fact that any religion can be practiced freely. We went through that area and that is why I entitled the article in that way. After the event in Zenica, since at about that time HVO carried out an attack near Kiseljak and Fojnica and took our lines, we received orders to go in the direction of Fojnica straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that there is a mistake in the transcript. Because it says that he allowed the military monastery. But the witness said that it was the guardian of the monastery in that period who was authorised to practice religion, and this was in 1463.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: May I just ask one last question. You referred to Fojnica and it's mentioned in this article that the entrance to Fojnica, Izetbegovic and his entourage passed by the unit. Were you, yourself, present when this encounter between Mr. Izetbegovic and the unit occurred, and when was it?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes. But we had left Zenica, but he stayed at Zenica. We marched across the mountain. There was snow on the ground. And when we were descending in that column, our column of soldiers, then Alija Izetbegovic with his entourage caught up with us. He was pleased because when we entered Fojnica, Fojnica had already been emptied. People had fled. And what little population was left there, when they heard that we were coming, they were pleased. I know that one woman came to me saying she was bringing out fruit and Alija was waiving to us from his Jeep and they went down to Fojnica and presumably continued in the direction of Sarajevo. We too got to Fojnica. We organised the defence lines and somewhere halfway up the mountain - I can't remember exactly the name of the mountain - that's where we stopped the advance of the HVO and that's the way it remained until a truce agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to switch the topic. You reported in 1993 as assistant commander of morale to your battalion commander and you stated his name already. Is it correct to say that you were also reporting, in 1993, to the assistant commander for morale and information of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Occasionally I would get certain orders from him; for example, I've mentioned the case of -- with Vares, Sulejman Kurtanovic. The reason why we did not have more of a communication was that we were physically separated. We were in two totally different towns. And we almost always were involved in some kind of war activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I may just ask for the name of the assistant commander for morale and information in the 7th Muslim mountain brigade, your superior there. Is his name Ahmet Adilovic?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: No. His name was Sulejman Kurtanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And he was on the brigade, in the brigade command of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Kurtanovic, Sulejman, we were together in Vares, that's what I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I may ask. You have stated your military career to us. Before you served in the 7th Muslim mountain brigade in November 1992, did you serve in any other unit in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The beginning of the war was marked by a very confused situation, and those units were being set up all over Bosnia. For the most part they were made up of volunteers who did not want to flee. They wanted to fight. And when I heard that one such unit was being set up within the framework of which there would be one part dedicated to religion, and this was something that attracted me as a man of faith, I made enquiries and I got the relevant information and then I joined that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please state the name of that unit, and its location.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And when did you join the Muslim forces in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: At some point in the beginning of June, I believe. On the 5th or the 6th of June, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it correct you're talking about the Muslimanske Snage in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to take you now back to 1993 when you were assistant commander for morale in the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. You testified that you were in the Bila valley from approximately April or mid-April to mid-June, 1993. Have you ever heard about incidents committed by members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, in the Bila valley in that time period?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: There were no members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, because I suppose what you mean is foreign nationals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. I'm actually referring to any member. Any soldier within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. I didn't mention foreign nationals, just did you hear that any soldiers from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were committing isolated or were committing incidents in that time period?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I did point out that after my departure and the departure of another group of soldiers from Travnik, after Ahmici and before Miletici, we joined that region defence sector. So we had a command and the location where we were was known precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So can you just clarify. Did you hear certain incidents? Or didn't you hear any incident at all? I couldn't get this from your answer.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear, as everyone else down in that valley, that something had happened. But establishing a link between that and the members of the 7th Muslim brigade did not really make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So your testimony is, you heard about incidents but you didn't hear about links. I was actually just asking for whether any soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were ever involved in that time period in incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that this line of questioning is confusing the witness. If my learned colleague wants to ask such a question, he should refer to a specific incident and provide the date and time of the incident concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Which incident are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution is actually not referring to any particular incident. The Prosecution is simply interested whether the witness has heard anything, an isolated incident, since he was based in the Bila valley or at the entrance of the Bila valley or at the entrance of the Bila Valley, in Alihodza, from what I understand. And the Prosecution is simply asking, since he was on the ground in that particular time period, whether the witness has heard anything. If he hasn't heard anything, that's fine. There is -- I'm not asking for a particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, a new incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On a number of occasions the Prosecution has told us that they're exercising their right to cross examine a witness, but in this case we really don't know what the Prosecution is trying to do. If they're trying to undermine the witness's credibility, they have to say "We have such-and-such information and we believe that you claimed the contrary or that you are going to claim the contrary." If the Prosecution wants to obtain information from the witness to support its own case, this is something that they have to do pursuant to Rule 90 of the Rules and they have to mention the evidence that they are seeking. They have to put its case to the witness, as one says in English. But the Prosecution is on a fishing expedition and this is leading nowhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given Rule 90 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, bearing that Rule in mind the witness said that he was familiar with the incident. To save time ask him about the incident concerned and then you may refresh his memory if there is any other information that we have. We are currently wasting time. I have to point that out to you

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please mention the incident or an incident you heard about which involved a member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in the Bila valley in 1993, during your tenure as assistant commander for morale. If you don't remember an incident, please just state so, I am prepared to move on.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: No. I don't remember an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you, during the time period you were assistant commander for morale in the 1st Battalion, have you heard that certain soldiers from the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade broke away from their unit?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Well, there was a somewhat long story. After the events in Visoko, before the New Year in 1992, when a fierce attack was launched against us, certain individuals somehow separated themselves in a way that was not obvious. They weren't happy with the command. So some of those individuals, two such individuals -- well, for some of those individuals, they didn't want to find themselves among our soldiers, because they would carry out all sorts of acts that were not in accordance with the code that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please refer to -- you mentioned certain individuals. Do you recall any names of these certain individuals? Just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Ramo Durmis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What do you know about Ramo Durmis?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As far as I could judge him, he was a very willful man. He had his own opinions. This is very dangerous, especially in wartime conditions. When it's necessary to listen to or to abide by the orders issued by the command. When I arrived in Visoko, I saw that he had been involved in a number of excesses, and he had placed himself in a position to be, in some way, removed, set aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned he was involved in some excesses in Visoko. What did you see when you came to Visoko? You mentioned you were there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I was supposed to carry out what the first group was supposed to carry out, but I was in the second group where we heard that the line had been penetrated, so we set off in a good mood. We wanted to raise the blockade of Sarajevo. We were aware of the situation that people were in over there. However, in the course of the day the situation changed. And when I arrived there, I entered some sort of a bowling hall or some sort of a sports hall, I don't know what it was exactly. But when I arrived there, I was shocked so to speak. Many people had died people who were there spoke to me about such things and they also mentioned what Durmis, Ramo had done. He had physically assaulted certain officers, believing that they were responsible for what had happened. Rumour had it that he had also reached for his weapon. That's something that could not have been tolerated according to the code that we had, regardless of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, can we have document -- Prosecution Exhibit P610 distributed. This is a document dating 4 August 1993 from Mr. Ahmet Adilovic. And I'm referring to number 4(b) of this document. This is on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to read out loud the text after number 4(b).

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: "A number of experienced and exceptionally good soldiers broke away from our unit with Ramo Durmis and Malik Basic, and the soldiers of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade want them returned to our force, if that is at all possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: First of all, I want to ask you, have you heard about this incident, that they broke away? I mean ...

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered the question, but the witness had previously confirmed that Ramo Durmis had left the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution, you are asking this question because there is a purpose that you have? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have only one question left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you recall the time period when Ramo Durmis and his people broke away from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: After what had happened in Visoko, I saw Ramo Durmis very rarely. I don't even know what the details are. I, at the time I did not have much information. I would gradually receive the information. I wasn't at the site. However, from the time these excesses were committed, relations turned cold. As far as I could understand, he asked -- or he was trying to find other men who shared his same opinion in order to attempt to do something with them, because it was quite obvious that he wasn't satisfied with the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
