utterances.text: This document is from August 1993. And when was this Visoko operation? Can you please give a time period.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The New Year of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So according to your knowledge, did he break away directly after New Year 1992? Or did he break away in early August 1993, since this document is dating from the 4th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: He was trying to find men who shared his opinion and he certainly needed some time to find such men. In August, that was after the events and with the HVO in the Bila valley. Throughout that period of time he wasn't under our command, as far as I can remember. Whatever he did, he did on his own initiative. He certainly took some other members of our battalion with him who followed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And these members from the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, do you recall whether this was from the 1st Company, from the 2nd company, or from the 3rd company? I'm just asking. It states here in the text from the 1st Company. But can you confirm this? Actually, it states here in the text, "the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade." Do you know whether it is -- from which company of the 1st Battalion these soldiers broke away?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I can't remember those details now. We were constantly on the move. At that time it was still possible to move from one unit to another, especially in the case of volunteer units. Men would try to see whether certain units suited them. If it didn't suit them, the men would leave. And it is now very difficult to remember all those faces and all of those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I thank you for answering all my questions. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could DK29 be shown to the witness, please. I have a copy for the witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You can have a look at the document. Could you have a look at the document, sir. It's dated the 19th of February, 1993. Could you have a look at the company commanders listed in the document.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Seferovic Basic, Rusovic Podek [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Company. What's his name?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Mesud, Seferovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: No, Muhamed Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Ramo Durmis was the commander of the 1st Company up until December when that operation in Visoko occurred?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I think he was in charge of a group because we started by establishing combat groups. That was at the beginning of the war. And the tactics were good until the lines had been established. And this is a system that we inherited to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the document dated the 19th of February, does this document show that Ramo Durmis was not the company of the first company in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have no further questions, Mr. President. But the word "company commander" is missing from the transcript. Page 48, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President I have just one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibranovic, I would just like to clarify something when answering questions about incidents that may have occurred involving members of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, you provided your answer. All I would like to do is ask you the following question. Would you agree with me if I said that members of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade were all Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no foreigners in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: They would occasionally appear and move around, but they couldn't oblige us to do anything and we couldn't oblige them to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They weren't members of the 7th Muslim brigade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: No. They weren't on our records.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have a few questions for you and there is one question that follows on the answer that you have just provided us with us. You said some foreigners would occasionally appear in the 7th Brigade. Could you provide us with any additional information. Who were these foreigners? Were they from the north, the south, the east, the west, and what were they doing in the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Well, given what one could learn through contact with them, they either introduced themselves as members of humanitarian organisations or as people who had come to assist. But in light of what I mentioned a while ago, there were certain disagreements because you can't come to assist me and take my heart at the same time. You want to help me, but I'm supposed to do what you want me to do. And for this reason, they caused us many problems in our communities. People were divided because they came with their own interpretation of Islam, which was not appropriate for our area, or did not fit in with our tradition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that these individuals caused problems, was this because they were soldiers in 7th Brigade units? Or were they outside the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: They weren't members of any brigades. They weren't obliged to act in any particular way. At one point they would be in one area. At another point in another area. They would move around Bosnia. And the problems they caused were as follows. They acted in the following way: I want to help you, but you have to change your religious tradition, your way of thinking, what you practice. And on the whole, this is why we couldn't see eye to eye. For example, there are situations in which Hasan would listen to one of the members of those humanitarian organizations. He would then receive food or something like that and would then come into conflict with his parents because he would start to perform rites in accordance with the rites that these Arabs perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever have the opportunity of speaking to these individuals?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as religion is concerned, did you have the impression that their religious training was more or less equivalent to the sort of training that you had? Or were these individuals people who didn't have the religious background that you yourself had? They didn't have the sort of education in religious matters that you yourself had?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I had the impression that they had left their homes and they had transplanted their local practices in our area. When I referred to this booklet a while ago, when I referred to science, science requires firm evidence, if claims of any kind are to be made. However, since these individuals came from all walks of life, there were labourers there too, well imagine such a situation, if you have to discuss religious matters with such a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question for you. As a member of the clergy when you were a member of the 7th Brigade, did you wear a uniform? Or were you in civilian clothes? Or in religious robes? Or did you have a uniform? Did you perhaps carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I had an ordinary uniform, just like all the other soldiers. While I was in the army, we didn't even have any particular ranks. It wasn't possible to distinguish us on the basis of our ranks. And as far as weapons are concerned, I had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, who was the commander of the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Changes were made, given the information we obtained in Travnik initially Asim Koricic was or should have been the commander and then he suddenly left. He went on some sort of a trip. I don't know the details, because I was in the field. And later, Kubura took up that position. There were frequent changes. It depended on the time and the situation and that was the case at the battalion level too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will move on to my last topic, that of Vares. As far as we have understood your testimony, you entered Vares. You don't know the exact date because first you said in October and then later the month of November was mentioned. So the exact date of entry into Vares is a little vague. But when you entered Vares, were you and the other soldiers the only ABiH soldiers who entered the town? Or were there any other army units there?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Given the situation I found there, the local police were present. I think that they were from the town and under local authorities. And at the same time we had information, according to which the 2nd Corps was coming from the north. We called them the "Tuzla Men," although I personally never met them. We stayed there for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But about the first BiH army soldiers who entered Vares, were they from your unit? Were you the first ones to enter Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: From my unit, I entered myself with a couple of other members of the command and I walked down the main street. I walked on foot. I've already mentioned the fact that there were some 50 young men there as well. And they stayed behind in that area. And when I came back from the upper town to the lower part of town, I found them there in an area where the UNPROFOR forces were. I've already mentioned that before. Apart from those local police officers who entered before we did, I don't know in what way because -- but we found them there, but apart from them, I did not mean -- meet anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you entered with your 50 men, were you -- I was going to say the highest-ranking officer, but at any rate, the person who had the highest degree of responsibility? Or was there another officer who had higher authority than you did? Or was it you? Were you the person in charge of those 50 soldiers? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Well, no. There was battalion commander there, Junosovic. I had already mentioned him as well. Let me reiterate once again I went to the upper part of the main street and I saw two buildings on fire, I believe, and I visited the mosque. And then I came back to the lower part of town where our fighters were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can you explain the fact that there were two buildings on fire? Who had set fire to those buildings because apparently you're saying when you entered Vares, the town was basically deserted. There were no HVO fighters there, so who had set those buildings on fire.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: According to the information I received, the HVO forces, as they were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you left Vares, as far as you know, were there any other buildings on fire or you only remember those two buildings being on fire?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Just those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just a few clarifying questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge has asked you about the presence of senior commanders in Vares or in the Vares area. To the best of your recollection where was the brigade command or the brigade commander during the Vares operation? Was he out of town, was he in town, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: At Strijezevo, the village where we came and stopped. It's somewhat larger village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So early in the morning when you with your 50 soldiers started to go to Vares, the brigade commander remained behind in Strijezevo?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I suppose so. I suppose. Because we did not meet until the next reporting perhaps, when the facts had been established, that is to say the HVO forces had fled. There was no combat activity. The city was full. And we had to decide what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said "we have not met until the next reporting." Can you please clarify, when did you, for the last time, meet him before you descended down to Vares? Was this hours before you left? Or was it days before you left to descend towards Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: It was a bit dark when we started from Strijezevo Celo, which is at a higher altitude. So we had to go down. We went down a narrow path which zig-zagged in the direction of the canyon. It was impossible to see anything whatsoever at that stage or observe anything of any consequence. Our command was to go straight ahead. We found mines on the road down there, but apparently the HVO had planned to have the rocks falling and then blocking the road. At a crossroads - I can't remember what the name of the crossroads is - there was a Muslim house there. And we stopped there and we waited for further commands. But when people heard that we were there, they went back to their house straight away and said -- we left. And then we just walked straight a head on the main road from that crossroads. I can't remember the name. Han or Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Majdan, meaning the suburb of Vares? Were you just referring to Majdan?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the precise name. It is a place where one road branches off to Vares, to the left, and I don't know where the right hand road goes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But to follow up on my previous question, I had asked you along the lines of the Presiding Judge who was asking for senior commanders. Where did you last meet the brigade commander before you descended to Vares? Was this in Strijezevo, just please clarify. I didn't get it from your answer.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: When we met the last time. It is a bit difficult for me to remember because for the most part we were all housed up there at that place. The commander from my battalion, I remember, was in a holiday home, that belonged to some kind of director or manager. We had communication, we were not too far away. But as to when exactly the last meeting took place, it's a bit difficult for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to clarify. You're talking about the commander of your battalion. Not the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade? You just mentioned commander "from my battalion," on line 55 -- on page 55, line 12. You're referring now to the commander of your battalion which you last met before you descended?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me about the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That's in your answer. On page 55, line 12, the -- you are stating "commander from my battalion." He was in a holiday home. But indeed I was asking you for the commander of the 7th Muslim mountain brigade, when you for the last time met him, before you descended towards Vares.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Look, that's not my level, as it were. I had links to the battalion. The assistant commander for the brigade, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: One last question relating to Vares. On page 55, line 8, you reported, I assume, about your return from Vares. And I had asked you when you met the commander and you stated, on page 54, line 8: We have not -- and I quote "We have not met until the reporting." Did you report back to anybody upon your return from Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Those of us who were the battalion assistant commanders for morale, we had meetings with the assistant commander of the brigade for morale. And that was when we met and when we exchanged that information, as to further plans and to the further development of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you recall what you reported once you were returning? What did you report about the situation in Vares?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The city was full of provisions. It was also full of stuff which was not of any consequence to us, such as alcohol and cigarettes. But there were still this problem of logistics, how to get the provisions to the soldiers for the upcoming activities since we had no means of transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So how did you solve -- or did you discuss the transport problem on the meeting of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My first comment is that this is outside the framework that you have determined. And secondly, my learned friend has already asked the same questions in the course of his cross-examination. The witness has already replied to those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have heard the comment. I am not going to deal with matters of transport. Move on to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will move to another subject. The President of the Trial Chamber has asked you about your encounters or your meetings with foreigners. And you said, indeed, occasionally -- or at least you had met some foreigners. I just wanted to ask you: Approximately how many foreigners did you talk to in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: About the number, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm referring not to -- just for clarification -- not to your encounters with UNPROFOR or people from Croatia. I'm referring to Mujahedin, persons, foreigners who called themselves Mujahedin or who were considered by the locals to be Mujahedin. I'm just asking how many such foreigners did you meet in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As to a specific number, I can't really name that, because I was mostly banned to a certain area. So that those things that happened in the hinterland, as it were, went straight over my head, in the sense that some information I only found out about after the war or maybe even now, even though recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You were referring to the hinterland. I assume you were referring to the Bila Valley area where you were in 1993. In the Bila Valley, how many foreign Mujahedin did you encounter in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The places they went to was Mehurici. And if you look at the map, it's seven to eight kilometres away from Alihodza. So we were physically separated. And going anywhere was risky business, really, even if anyone were to attempt to reach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand. But you told the Presiding Judge that you, indeed, met some Mujahedin. Where did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Those meetings were nothing special. They were not especially agreed or they were not in a specific place. They could have happened in the street, or in the country, or in the middle of the road. I mean, exchanging views about certain matters. But I've already said that we simply could not find a common language to speak about these matters because, in that - what should I call it - in this somewhat more extreme version or interpretation of Islam, they even go as far as to say -- for example they will say: You're religion is incorrect. It's not all right. And when you hear these things, then you can't really have any sort of dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You're now talking about the different perceptions of religion. If I may ask. The foreigners you met, were they from Sunni faith or from Shia faith?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: For the most part they were Sunnis, a couple of Shiites. That's a historic quandary, really. A problem that I perhaps shouldn't go into now, but what is of essence is this. This is the whole root of all the problems we're seeing today. An attitude to one thing. Muslims living in Europe obviously bring along their own culture the way it is, and their religion. But somebody who lives in the East, they have their own views. And when these two groups, as it were, meet obviously there are problems and you have to take account of the fact, okay, this guy is coming from the Orient and then you want to help us out. But if you cause more trouble than it's worth, then there is a question mark over the whole thing then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the majority of the foreigners you spoke to were Sunnis? In the Bila Valley, of those people you happened to meet?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: In my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is not a correctly put question, because the witness has already replied that he could have met these people passing by in the street, in the country. He never once mentioned the Bila Valley. And, therefore, the question in the way it has been put does not really reflect the witness's answer to the previous question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm prepared to withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember any names or pseudonyms, these people gave themselves, like "Abu," and so on, these people you spoke to.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I do remember some. Although what you're saying is something I found out later on. Those were codes, in fact, because they were hiding their real names. And that too tends to corroborate the fact that this kind of mixing is likely to cause a great deal of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you state -- state some of these names?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: I was present at an autopsy, after an event either at Ahmici, or thereabouts, one of those Arabs had been killed and his name was Abu Sahar. His body near to my community. Just one detail. I mean, apparently he was still alive and then he died on the way to hospital, and a committee of enquiry was set up to investigate the case and I was a member of that committee and we looked at the body. I think he took about seven bullets from a pistol at close range. So Abu Sahar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you have any other names?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: In the beginning of the war, I met somebody who was Abu Sahar, I can't remember. He was the first person I met, and he was killed at Visoko in 1992, in the summer of 1992, sometime in July or August. That's what I heard. The line was at Karazici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the place very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the place, please, where the body was found.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: Cekrcic. It's a bit difficult. C-e-k-r-c-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please also, for the record, state the place where Abu Sahar was found. You said your community. Can you please just state in which location he was found.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: So we were looking at the map earlier on. My community is made up of three parts: Zelote, Alihodza, and Karahodze. In the vicinity of Karahodze there is a bridge which is called the Zukic Bridge. And he was thrown off the road and he was wrapped in a blanket. And one of the people working in the fields noticed that and reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My last question is, you stated you were in a commission investigating this incident and you also talked about the other dead body near Visoko. Did you find any documentation on the bodies of the corpses of these dead foreigners?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: As to Abu Sahar at Visoko, I only heard the information about him. So I don't know exactly. I was told about the location and, as to Abu Sahar, I was present. No documents were found on him. I think everything he had had been taken. I had the impression that he had been robbed, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned to the Presiding Judge that you met some Mujahedin. Now you gave us the -- two incidents which involved more or less dead Mujahedin. I see my colleague on their feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This line of questioning may confuse the witness. When the learned colleague was asking the question, he asked whether the witness heard of incidents in which members of the 7th Muslim Brigade participated, whereas now this obviously has no link to the questions he had asked before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm just asking a follow-up question relating to the Judge's -- or Your Honour's question, which related to contacts which this witness had with Mujahedin. I'm not following up on questions I put during my cross-examination. So with the leave of the Trial Chamber, I would put one last question relating to potential -- mere encounters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last question now, because time is ticking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember any names of foreign Mujahedin which you met, if allow me, while they were alive.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The one who died at Visoko, I met him whilst he was alive, Buzuhera [phoen] because when he came at some point mid-June it was a rather exclusive event in Bosnia. Consider the situation we were in. All this murder and persecution going on and then all of a sudden somebody comes along to help you. And since our people is good and welcoming, certainly they were willing to host people who came along to help. So it was at some point mid June. He moved to Visoko I think in August, that was my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Am I allowed to ask a last question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in discussion with the Presiding Judge the religious -- or the different religions who met through the foreigners coming to Bosnia and the local religion practiced there. And you have also mentioned Sufism. Is Sufism part of the Sunni faith or of the Shiite faith?

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: The Sunni faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one question to make everything clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In response to a question put to the witness by the Presiding Judge, page 49, line 24, you said that these foreign combatants weren't members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: Dzemail Ibranovic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this completes your testimony. On behalf of the judges, I thank you for having you come to testify at The Hague at the request of the Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura. I wish you a safe trip home and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we adjourn, since I think that we're almost at the end of the tape, does the Defence counsel have a witness available for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness scheduled for tomorrow is ready and, if everything runs smoothly, I think we will be able to finish with the witness tomorrow and it won't be necessary to have a hearing on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in any event, we can't have a hearing on Friday, since we've taken note of your wish not to have a hearing -- or not to have hearings scheduled for Friday. We have a few more minutes. Would either of the parties like to raise any issues? Mr. Mundis. No problems? No questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No problems. No questions. No issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. As far as the Defence is concerned the situation must be identical?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you in that case and invite you all to attend the hearing that will commence tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
